FUEL TAX HOLIDAY IN AMERICA: 

US states are taking significant actions to lower gasoline and diesel prices via either tax-holidays and/or allowing the use of dyed diesel on highways. 

Some of tax holidays are large: Ohio, for example, is about to suspend a ~40 cents per gallon state tax on gas and diesel. Other states are using dyed diesel as a way to offer tax relief, including Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri, Alabama, Nebraska and Louisiana.

Europe is finding itself sandwiched from all sides when it comes to refined products — diesel in particular (some of the damage is due to the US-Iran war; some is due to Ukraine-Russia; some is due to China, and a lot is self-inflicted). Policy response: Head in the sand.

CHART OF THE DAY: While crude flows from Persian Gulf nations (ex Iran) have recovered to 80% of pre-war levels, the same is not true for refined products. Their exports of gasoline, jet-fuel, and diesel, remain at around 50% of pre-war levels.

September produced a striking divergence between #gold and investment demand. Gold fell as US Treasury #yields surged, yet gold ETF holdings rose for a second consecutive month. The continued inflows suggest investors were looking beyond the immediate headwind from higher real yields and instead focusing on what those higher borrowing costs may ultimately mean for fiscal sustainability and already elevated government debt levels. It raises an interesting question: what happens to gold once yields stabilise and the inflationary impulse from higher energy prices begins to fade? If investment demand has remained resilient during such a hostile rates environment, an easing of that pressure could provide a powerful tailwind. 
Chart source: Bloomberg
